title: AST Reference Methods, Method Agreement and the Antibiogram
summary: Learn why broth microdilution is the reference AST method, how a gradient strip MIC is read, how a new method is judged by essential and categorical agreement and very major or major errors, and how CLSI M39 builds an antibiogram from first isolates only.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 58 Hits 2, 11, 15 and 20 and Trap 6. Checked against Gajic 2022 and Gajdács 2017 (open full text), Humphries 2018, Simner 2022 and Horvat 2003 (each read via a page-fetch tool), Klinker 2021 and Tran 2023. The reviewer cites CLSI M39-A4 (2014); the current edition is M39 5th edition (2022), with the same core rules (register flag rv-ch58-m39-edition). The first-isolate rule can underestimate resistance (rv-ch58-first-isolate-underestimate). The ≥90% essential-agreement target is confirmed from the CLSI working group best-practice paper; its attribution to CLSI M52 verification could not be checked because M52 is not openly available (rv-ch58-ea-m52). The reviewer’s BMD conditions (35 °C, ambient air, 16–20 h) were not confirmed: the review read gives “at least 16–24 h” and CLSI M07 was not accessible (rv-ch58-bmd-incubation), so incubation conditions are not taught. Not taught: Etest use for pneumococcal penicillin MICs, “elliptical” zone wording, M52 specifics.

objectives: Identify broth microdilution as the reference AST method and agar dilution as the anaerobe gold standard.
Read a gradient strip MIC correctly, including the between-marks and haemolysis rules.
Define essential agreement, categorical agreement, very major, major and minor errors, and state the ≥90% agreement targets.
Apply the CLSI M39 rules for building an antibiogram, including first-isolate deduplication and its limitation.

cues.text: Three items wait on the quality desk. A new automated susceptibility panel agrees with broth microdilution, within one doubling dilution, for eighty-eight percent of MICs.
A draft antibiogram counts every Staphylococcus aureus culture, and one ICU patient was cultured twenty times.
And a gradient strip’s zone crosses the strip between two marks. Pass, recount, or which MIC?

scenes.title: Reference methods and the gradient strip
scenes.altText: Schematic: three method cards. Broth microdilution (BMD) card: twofold serial dilutions of each drug in 96-well microtitre plates, each well inoculated with a standardised inoculum; the MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth; BMD is the reference (“gold standard”) method recommended by CLSI and EUCAST, and for some drugs, such as colistin, the only appropriate MIC method. Agar dilution card: drug incorporated into agar plates; the gold standard for anaerobes (CLSI M11 lists agar dilution and broth microdilution as anaerobe reference methods); labour-intensive, suited to reference laboratories. Gradient strip card: a plastic or paper strip carries a predefined continuous antibiotic gradient; the MIC is read where the zone of inhibition intersects the strip scale; if the intersection falls between two marks, the higher value is reported; reading at the edge of β-haemolysis gives falsely high MICs.

cues.text: Broth microdilution is the reference method recommended by CLSI and EUCAST. Twofold dilutions of each drug sit in a 96-well plate, each well gets a standardised inoculum, and the MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth.

For anaerobes, agar dilution is the gold standard. CLSI lists agar dilution and broth microdilution as the anaerobe reference methods, but agar dilution is labour-intensive and suits reference laboratories.
The gradient strip combines diffusion and dilution. A strip carries a predefined, continuous gradient of drug, and the MIC is read where the zone of inhibition meets the strip.

If the zone meets the strip between two marks, report the higher value. Do not read at the edge of beta-haemolysis, which gives a falsely high MIC. And for colistin, broth microdilution remains the only appropriate method.

scenes.title: Judging a new method against the reference
scenes.altText: Schematic agreement chart (CLSI Methods Development and Standardization Working Group, Humphries 2018). New-method results are compared with the CLSI BMD reference. Essential agreement (EA): the new MIC is within one log2 (doubling) dilution of the reference MIC; applies only to methods that give MICs. Categorical agreement (CA): same S/I/R category as the reference. Targets: EA ≥90% and CA ≥90%. Error cards: very major error (VME) = resistant isolate called susceptible (false susceptibility), the greatest concern, typically <3% of resistant isolates; major error (ME) = susceptible isolate called resistant, typically <3% of susceptible isolates; minor error = one result intermediate and the other S or R, ≤10%.

cues.text: A new susceptibility method is judged against the reference, broth microdilution. Essential agreement means the new MIC lands within one doubling dilution of the reference MIC. It only applies to methods that report MICs.

Categorical agreement means the same susceptible, intermediate or resistant category. CLSI best-practice targets are at least ninety percent essential agreement and at least ninety percent categorical agreement.
Then the errors. A very major error is a resistant isolate called susceptible: false susceptibility, the greatest concern, because the patient may get a drug that fails.

A major error is a susceptible isolate called resistant. A minor error involves the intermediate category. Very major and major errors are typically held below three percent, minor errors at ten percent or less.

scenes.title: Building an antibiogram
scenes.altText: Antibiogram rules card (CLSI M39, 5th edition, 2022, as summarised by Simner 2022): include only diagnostic (not surveillance) isolates; only final, verified results; only the first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period, regardless of specimen source or susceptibility profile; only species with ≥30 isolates; analyse and present at least annually. Evidence token (Horvat 2003): in one year at one university hospital, the MRSA rate was 39% with duplicate S. aureus isolates and 37% without; the authors note the pattern may not apply to other bacteria. Caveat token (Klinker 2021): the first-isolate rule may underestimate resistance, because a later resistant isolate from a patient whose first isolate was susceptible is not counted. Hook answers card: (1) 88% EA is below the ≥90% target; (2) count the 20-culture patient once; (3) report the higher strip value, 0.75.

cues.text: An antibiogram summarises percent susceptible for local use. CLSI M39, now in its fifth edition, says: diagnostic isolates only, not surveillance swabs; final verified results only; at least thirty isolates per species; and analysis at least once a year.

Duplicates are removed: only the first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period counts. In one year at one university hospital, the MRSA rate was thirty-nine percent with duplicates and thirty-seven percent without.
The rule has a cost: a patient whose first isolate was susceptible but who later grows a resistant one is not counted again, so resistance can be underestimated.
Back to the hook. Eighty-eight percent essential agreement misses the ninety percent target. The twenty-culture patient counts once. And the strip MIC is the higher mark, zero point seven five.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A very major error is a false resistant result” (✓ very major = resistant called susceptible, false susceptibility; major = false resistance); “Count every isolate in the antibiogram” (✓ first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period only); “Strip zone between two marks: round down” (✓ report the higher value).

cues.text: Trap one: a very major error is a false resistant result. No: very major is false susceptibility, a resistant isolate called susceptible. False resistance is a major error.
Trap two: count every isolate in the antibiogram. No: only the first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period.
Trap three: when a strip zone falls between two marks, round down. No: report the higher value.

In the antibiogram, ONE PATIENT, ONE VOTE.” Tokens: referee = BMD · one step, nine in ten · one patient, one vote. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: broth microdilution is the referee. A new method must land within one step of the referee nine times in ten. Very major is very dangerous: it calls a resistant bug susceptible. And in the antibiogram, one patient, one vote.
Where it breaks: agar dilution is the referee for anaerobes; essential agreement only applies to methods that give MICs; and one vote per patient can hide resistance that develops later.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “BMD = reference · EA within ±1 dilution ≥ 90% · CA ≥ 90% · very major = false susceptible”, “Antibiogram: first isolate per patient per period · ≥ 30 isolates · at least annually”.

cues.text: Broth microdilution is the reference that new methods must match, with at least ninety percent of MICs within one doubling dilution and very few very major errors, and an antibiogram counts only the first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period.

props.label: BMD = reference · EA ±1 dilution ≥ 90% · very major = false S

explanation.what: Plain language: one standard test, broth microdilution, is the yardstick every other susceptibility test is measured against. A new test must give nearly the same MIC most of the time and must almost never call a resistant bug susceptible. A hospital’s yearly susceptibility summary counts each patient once per organism so that repeatedly cultured patients do not dominate it. Scientific terms: broth microdilution (BMD), agar dilution, gradient diffusion strip, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), essential agreement (EA), categorical agreement (CA), very major error (VME), major error (ME), minor error, cumulative antibiogram, CLSI M39, first-isolate rule.
explanation.why: A false-susceptible result can send a patient onto a drug that will fail, so it is weighted as the worst error. Some patients are cultured again and again (in one university-hospital study, patients with MRSA had more repeat isolates than those with MSSA); without deduplication their isolates over-weight the percentages, which in that study raised the calculated MRSA rate.
explanation.measure: EA: new MIC within ±1 doubling dilution of the reference MIC (MIC methods only). Targets EA ≥90%, CA ≥90%; VME typically <3% of resistant isolates; ME typically <3% of susceptible isolates; minor errors ≤10%. Gradient strip: read where the zone meets the strip; between two marks, report the higher; not at the β-haemolysis edge. Antibiogram (M39, 5th ed.): diagnostic isolates, final verified results, first isolate per species per patient per period, ≥30 isolates, at least annually.
explanation.differs: Very major (false susceptible) vs major (false resistant) vs minor (involves I); EA (MIC level) vs CA (category); BMD (general reference) vs agar dilution (anaerobe gold standard); deduplicated vs raw antibiogram.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: decide whether 88% EA passes, name the most dangerous error type, choose which isolates enter an antibiogram, or read a strip MIC that falls between marks.

mnemonic.text: Broth microdilution is the REFEREE. A new method must land within ONE step of the referee NINE times in TEN. VERY major is VERY dangerous: it calls a resistant bug susceptible. In the antibiogram, ONE PATIENT, ONE VOTE.
mnemonic.explanation: Referee = reference method; one step, nine in ten = EA within one dilution ≥90%; one patient, one vote = first-isolate rule.

questions.stem: A new automated AST panel is compared with broth microdilution. 88% of its MICs are within one doubling dilution of the reference, and no very major errors occur. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: Essential agreement is below the ≥90% target, so performance is not acceptable
options.rationale: Correct. Essential agreement within ±1 doubling dilution should be at least 90%.

options.text: Acceptable, because there were no very major errors
options.rationale: Incorrect. Error rates and agreement are separate criteria; both must be met.

options.text: Acceptable, because 85% essential agreement is the target
options.rationale: Incorrect. The target is at least 90%, not 85%.

options.text: Essential agreement cannot be calculated for an MIC method
options.rationale: Incorrect. Essential agreement applies only to methods that report MICs, so it is exactly the right measure here.

questions.stem: A patient in intensive care has Staphylococcus aureus isolated from 20 cultures during one year. How should these isolates enter that year’s antibiogram?

options.text: Only the first isolate of S. aureus from that patient in the analysis period is counted
options.rationale: Correct. CLSI M39 removes duplicates by including only the first isolate of a species per patient per analysis period.
Incorrect. Repeat isolates over-weight frequently cultured patients and can shift the percentages.

options.text: Only the most resistant isolate is counted
options.rationale: Incorrect. The rule applies regardless of susceptibility profile; choosing by resistance would bias the data.

options.text: Only surveillance swab isolates are counted
options.rationale: Incorrect. Antibiograms include diagnostic isolates, not surveillance isolates.

questions.stem: Which result is a very major error when a new susceptibility method is compared with the reference method?

options.rationale: Correct. A very major error is false susceptibility, the error of greatest concern.
Incorrect. False resistance is a major error.
Incorrect. Disagreements involving the intermediate category are minor errors.

options.text: New MIC one doubling dilution above the reference, same category
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is within essential agreement and in categorical agreement; it is not an error.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer cites CLSI M39-A4 (2014); the current edition is M39 5th edition (2022). The core antibiogram rules taught here are unchanged.

The first-isolate rule limits duplicate bias but can underestimate resistance, because later resistant isolates from patients whose first isolate was susceptible are excluded; duplicates are not shown to inflate resistance for every organism.

The ≥90% essential-agreement target was verified from the CLSI working group best-practice paper on evaluating AST; its attribution to CLSI M52 verification could not be checked because M52 is not openly available.

The reviewer gives BMD incubation as 35 °C in ambient air for 16–20 h; the open review read states incubation of at least 16–24 h, and CLSI M07 was not accessible. Incubation conditions are not taught.
